title: Three Landings on One Comet
summary: On 2 March 2004, a spacecraft began a journey that would last more than ten years.

paragraphs.text: On 2 March 2004, a spacecraft began a journey that would last more than ten years.
It was called Rosetta. Attached to it was a smaller machine, Philae, with legs that would eventually stand on a comet.

Comets were valuable targets because they preserved material from the early Solar System. Their ice, dust, and rocky ingredients could help scientists study the conditions in which planets had formed.
But visiting one was difficult.
A comet did not sit in a fixed place waiting for a spacecraft. It travelled around the Sun, sometimes at great speed, while its activity changed as sunlight warmed it.
Rosetta had to reach its destination and match its motion. Merely crossing the comet's path would produce a brief encounter. Following it required arriving with the right position and speed.
The mission used flybys of Earth and Mars to change Rosetta's course and speed. During these manoeuvres, the spacecraft exchanged a tiny amount of energy with moving planets.
The planets scarcely noticed. For Rosetta, the assistance was crucial.
Part of the journey carried it so far from the Sun that conserving energy became essential. Rosetta spent more than two years in hibernation before waking in January 2014.
Its destination was Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko.
As the spacecraft approached, the comet's shape became clearer. Instead of a simple ball, it had two large lobes joined by a narrow region. Cliffs, pits, boulders, and rough surfaces covered it.
There was no smooth runway for Philae.

Rosetta arrived in August 2014. Before sending down the lander, the team studied the comet to choose a location. They needed ground that was reasonably safe and enough sunlight for Philae's solar panels.
Those requirements did not always favour the same place. A location with good sunlight might have dangerous terrain. A sheltered location could leave the lander without enough power.
The comet was also turning. The chosen site moved with that rotation, so the timing and path of descent had to account for a landing place that would not stay still.
Philae could not be steered like a helicopter. Once released, it would fall toward the comet under the weak pull of gravity.
Weak gravity created a surprising difficulty.
On Earth, gravity holds a landed machine firmly against the ground. On a small comet, the downward pull is much weaker. A gentle landing could still make a machine bounce away.
Philae therefore carried equipment intended to secure it. Harpoons would fire into the surface, and screws in its feet were meant to help it grip.
On 12 November 2014, Rosetta released the lander.
For about seven hours, Philae descended. Rosetta continued flying nearby, carrying signals between the lander and Earth.
Messages took many minutes to cross the distance. By the time controllers learned something had happened, that moment was already in the past.
Philae touched the comet.
Its harpoons did not fire.
The lander bounced.
Because gravity was so weak, the bounce lasted far longer than an ordinary bounce on Earth. Philae travelled across the comet before touching it again.
It bounced a second time and finally settled at a third location.
The machine had landed, but it was no longer where the team intended. It stood in an awkward position, with much of its surroundings blocking sunlight.
That made its battery a deadline.
The first battery had been charged before separation. Once its energy was exhausted, the solar panels would need enough light to keep the lander working.
At the unexpected landing site, that supply was limited.

The team put the available hours to work. Philae measured its surroundings and returned images and scientific information. Its instruments examined properties of the surface and sampled material around the lander.

Scientists had to interpret the results carefully. An instrument's position mattered. A measurement made beside a shaded cliff meant something different from one made on the open surface originally chosen.
After roughly sixty hours of work, the lander ran short of power and became silent.
Rosetta remained active.
It followed the comet as it moved closer to the Sun. Warming ice released gas, carrying dust into space. Rosetta could observe changes that a fast flyby would have missed.
Philae briefly made contact again in June 2015 as conditions changed, but a dependable continuing connection was not established.
Meanwhile, the search for its final location continued.
Researchers used images, timing, magnetic measurements, and other information to reconstruct the bounces. Knowing where Philae stood was part of understanding its data.
In September 2016, Rosetta photographed the lander among the comet's rough terrain. Its tilted body and extended legs could finally be recognised in the images.
The small machine had been found.
Later that month, Rosetta's own mission ended with a controlled descent to the comet. As it approached, it collected more close-range information before communication stopped.
The mission had not unfolded exactly as planned. Philae's anchor system failed, the lander bounced, and the useful surface work was shortened by shadow.
Yet a spacecraft had followed a comet through changing seasons of sunlight, and a lander had sent measurements from its surface for the first time.
The scientists received more than spectacular pictures. They received evidence that would take years to study, including information about the comet's shape, chemistry, gases, and dust.
Philae's three touchdowns also revealed something about exploration on small worlds.
Landing was only the first part of the problem.
Remaining landed was another.
